title: What MCP changes about enterprise software
content:
What MCP changes about enterprise software
For the past 20 years, enterprise software was judged by what users saw: usability, workflow, onboarding and training. Buyers picked the products that they believed their teams would actually use.
That’s changing.
A user can now type a request into a chat interface, an agent can call several systems behind the scenes, and an answer appears. Multiple vendors did the work. The user opened none of their apps.
Gartner estimates that up to $234 billion in enterprise application spending could be exposed to agents completing tasks across systems by 2030.
That raises a harder question: Which jobs should a general-purpose AI handle itself, and which are better left to a specialist?
We put that question to Marcus Tober, Semrush's SVP AI & Innovation, and Steven Syrek, who leads DeepL's work on agentic experience.
Intelligence is only part of the job
Ask a general-purpose model to do specialist work, and it often has to reason its way there from scratch, reading the context, inferring the rules, and checking the output. That reasoning is billed as it happens, so cost grows with usage and complexity.
A specialist system is built the other way around. The workflow is defined, domain expertise is built in, and the cost and output are easier to predict.
"Our product is not a UI or an app or a website," Syrek says. "It's actually a set of capabilities, and our customers don't need to care how those are implemented."
That distinction matters more as agents become the interface. General-purpose models provide reasoning, while specialist systems provide a capability built for a specific job.
So was the SaaSpocalypse wrong?
The "SaaSpocalypse" thesis was simple: If frontier models can reason through any workflow, and anyone can vibe-code a wrapper around it in a single weekend, why keep paying for specialist tools?
Tober argues that this underestimated what comes after the prototype.
"Everyone is a builder now, and most things can be assembled in a few vibe-coding sessions," he says. "The enterprise bill arrives afterwards: legal compliance, ISO 27001, security, stability and a guarantee the software is still maintained in three years. Maintenance is the cost, and it never stops."
AI has made software easier to build, but it hasn’t removed the cost of making it reliable, secure and maintainable at an enterprise scale.
Where MCP fits: The seam, not the story
None of this requires picking a side. It requires a way for one to call on the other.
That's where the Model Context Protocol (MCP) comes in. MCP gives AI agents a standardized way to connect all external tools and capabilities, reducing the need for custom integrations for every combination.
MCP is the practical answer to the "build vs. buy vs. embed" question. The generalist assistant can stay at the front door, and when a task needs a specialist capability, it can call on that system directly.
"What changes," Syrek explains, "is the number of places a customer can reach your capabilities." Not because the interface changes, but because it stops needing to.
What’s emerging now looks less like one model swallowing the other, and more like a division of labor where general-purpose systems can handle reasoning and orchestration, while specialist systems do the jobs they are built for. The MCP connects the two.
We recently launched the DeepL MCP Server, bringing DeepL’s Language AI capabilities directly into AI assistants like Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude, as well as other compatible tools.

report.summary: MCP standardizes how AI agents call specialist enterprise tools, shifting software value from user interfaces to embedded, maintainable domain capabilities.
report.background: For two decades, enterprise software competed on user experience: onboarding, workflow design, and adoption. Buyers chose tools their teams would actually open. Agentic AI breaks that assumption. A user types one request into a chat interface, and an agent silently calls multiple back-end systems to produce an answer—without the user opening any vendor app. Gartner estimates up to $234 billion in enterprise application spending could be exposed to cross-system agents by 2030. This raises a strategic question: should general-purpose models handle everything, or should they orchestrate specialist systems? The 'SaaSpocalypse' thesis claimed frontier models and vibe-coded wrappers would destroy specialist SaaS. In practice, enterprises still need compliance, ISO 27001, security, stability, and multi-year maintenance—costs that prototypes ignore. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) emerges as the connective standard for a division of labor between reasoning models and specialist capabilities.
key_points: The agent interface changes what buyers evaluate. When users never open an app, usability and onboarding matter less than whether a system exposes reliable, callable capabilities. Vendors are judged by what their product can do, not how its UI looks.

General-purpose models and specialist systems have opposite cost structures. A frontier model reasons through specialist work from scratch, so inference costs scale with usage and complexity. A specialist system encodes domain workflows, making output and cost more predictable for repeatable enterprise tasks.

The 'SaaSpocalypse' thesis underestimated post-prototype costs. Anyone can assemble a wrapper in a weekend, but legal compliance, security audits, ISO 27001, stability, and long-term maintenance create an enterprise bill that never stops. These are the real moats for specialist vendors.

MCP acts as the standardized seam between generalist assistants and specialist tools. Instead of custom integrations for every model-tool combination, agents can discover and call external capabilities through one protocol, making 'build vs. buy vs. embed' a routing decision rather than an architectural rewrite.

Vendors gain reach, not obsolescence. As Syrek notes, what changes is the number of places a customer can reach your capabilities. DeepL's MCP Server brings Language AI into Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude, letting specialist systems participate in agent workflows without forcing users into a separate app.
report.impact: For the AI industry, MCP accelerates a shift from monolithic assistants to composable agent ecosystems. SaaS pricing may move from per-seat licenses toward usage-based or capability-based models, as value accrues to systems that agents actually call. For developers, the priority shifts from building polished UIs to exposing secure, well-documented MCP endpoints, with skills in auth, rate limiting, observability, and compliance becoming more valuable than front-end work. For regular users, tasks get faster and less app-switching, but new questions arise around trust, data governance, auditability, and which specialist system an agent chooses. Enterprises will demand agent-level permissions, logging, and vendor accountability before wide adoption. The winners will likely be platforms that combine strong reasoning with a vibrant network of reliable specialist MCP servers.
report.tools: Watch Anthropic's Model Context Protocol specification and reference servers for building MCP endpoints. DeepL MCP Server shows how specialist capabilities plug into Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude. Microsoft Copilot Studio and OpenAI's connector ecosystem support agent tool-calling. For local experimentation, Cursor and Claude Desktop can connect to MCP servers. Zapier MCP and open-source MCP servers on GitHub offer quick integration patterns. LangChain and LlamaIndex provide MCP adapters for custom agent pipelines.
